requirements.fact: Dry reeds shatter into jagged splinters and soaking basins create dangerous slip hazards.
requirements.misconception: Basket weaving materials are completely harmless because reeds contain no sharp motorized parts.
pamphlet_excerpts: Tool Handling Protocol: Always cut tough reed splints directly away from your body using shears.
Reed Soaking Caution: Excess soaking weakens natural fibers and creates hazardous slippery puddles on workshop floors.
Awl Safety Practice: Direct pointed bodkins into weaving channels while keeping fingers clear of tips.
Mold Prevention Rule: Hang damp cane bundles in well ventilated areas to prevent toxic mildew.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: Basketry tools require sharp utility shears, awls, and soaking tubs that introduce slip and puncture risks. Weavers manage moisture levels to prevent mold while maintaining organized cutting surfaces to avoid lacerations.
requirements.safety_callout: Carry shears closed with point down and wipe basin floor leaks immediately.
socratic_questions: How does moisture control prevent respiratory health problems during reed storage?
Why must you push an awl away from your supporting hand?
What immediate steps treat a deep puncture from a reed splitter?
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Setup Area: Position water tubs securely on stable benches beside dry towel staging mats.
Step 2 - Inspect Tools: Check cutting shears and packing tools for dull blades or loose joints.
Step 3 - Cut Materials: Trim rattan stakes across fiber grain using smooth single cuts with shears.
Step 4 - Clean Workshop: Wipe spilled water puddles and collect scrap reed off walking path surfaces.

sub_requirements.fact: Dull blades slip off round reed fibers, increasing the likelihood of painful hand injuries.
sub_requirements.misconception: Dull craft shears are safer than sharp shears when trimming thick basket stakes.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Working with reed shears, awls, and water basins presents puncture, cutting, and slip hazards. Weavers anticipate risks by organizing tools safely and wiping up water spills promptly.

sub_requirements.fact: Plant fibers carry soil bacteria and fungi that cause serious infections in untreated punctures.
sub_requirements.misconception: Minor reed cuts do not need washing because dry rattan fibers are naturally sterile.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Scrapes from rough reeds and punctures from awls require immediate cleaning and protection. Proper wound washing and sterile dressings prevent infections caused by organic plant matter.

requirements.fact: Stakes woven with round flexible reed weavers define wicker rather than flat plaiting.
requirements.misconception: All baskets with upright stakes belong strictly to the plaited construction classification.
pamphlet_excerpts: Plaited Structure Trait: Interlacing flat parallel splints creates checkerboard patterns across the basket wall.
Coiled Basket Method: Stitching spiraling bundles of grasses or pine needles builds dense waterproof vessels.
Ribbed Frame Design: Bending heavy hoops creates a rigid skeleton that supports woven infill reeds.
Wicker Craft Form: Weaving flexible round reed weavers through rigid upright spokes provides upright strength.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: Basketry traditions use plaited, coiled, ribbed, and wicker structures defined by specific core materials and weaving techniques. Weavers select distinct weaves such as twining, randing, and pairing to achieve desired strength and appearance.
requirements.safety_callout: Handle vintage or dry display baskets gently to prevent brittle splinters from flying.
socratic_questions: What mechanical difference separates a coiled basket foundation from a wicker base?
Why does twining produce a tighter fabric than simple over-under randing?
How does the rib placement in melon baskets dictate the overall shape?
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Examine Foundation: Identify whether the base uses flat splints, spiral coils, or wooden hoops.
Step 2 - Classify Structure: Determine if spokes remain upright or bend across a structural ribbed framework.
Step 3 - Analyze Weave: Trace whether weavers travel in single rows, paired twists, or triple braids.
Step 4 - Record Technique: Document the identified construction category and specific weave types in project notes.

sub_requirements.fact: Coiled baskets rely on continuous sewing stitches that bind successive rounds of core material.
sub_requirements.misconception: Coiled baskets use identical over-and-under weaving actions as wicker and ribbed baskets.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Baskets fall into four distinct construction categories based on foundation materials and fabrication mechanics. Plaited baskets use flat splints, coiled use stitched bundles, ribbed use intersecting hoops, and wicker uses rigid stakes with flexible weavers.

sub_requirements.fact: Pairing locks upright spokes in place and prevents outward bowing under heavy loads.
sub_requirements.misconception: Pairing and waling are purely decorative variations with zero added structural strength.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Weavers select distinct patterns including simple randing, pairing, and three-rod waling to achieve structural goals. Each weave controls spoke spacing, lateral tension, and decorative surface texture.

requirements.fact: Excessive tension pulls basket sides inward, distorting the intended functional vessel shape.
requirements.misconception: Tension should be pulled as tightly as possible during every side weaving row.
pamphlet_excerpts: Reed Hydration Timing: Soak flat reed fifteen minutes to achieve pliability before bending tight corners.
Spoke Upsetting Method: Score flat stakes lightly across fibers to bend basket sides upward cleanly.
Round Base Radiance: Space base spokes at equal radial angles before beginning fine twining rows.
Stool Splint Tension: Pull seating splints taut without warping the wooden chair frame inward.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: Building square baskets, round baskets, and campstools requires mastering layout, staking, weaving, and border finishing. Crafting functional articles demands proper material preparation, uniform tension, and secure locking borders.
requirements.safety_callout: Clamp wooden stool rails securely during weaving to prevent unexpected scissor pinches.
socratic_questions: Why must base stakes remain damp while upsetting the sides of a basket?
How does inserting an odd number of spokes enable continuous simple randing?
What secures the raw splint ends when weaving a herringbone campstool pattern?
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Soak Materials: Immerse reeds in warm water until fibers bend freely without cracking.
Step 2 - Lay Foundation: Weave the bottom grid or insert spokes into slotted wooden bases.
Step 3 - Weave Sides: Pack successive rows of weavers firmly downward using uniform hand tension.
Step 4 - Finish Rim: Fold down remaining spoke ends and lash rim strips securely around top.

sub_requirements.fact: Failing to score flat stakes causes ragged breaks and rounded, misshapen corners.
sub_requirements.misconception: Square basket corners form naturally without pre-bending or scoring the base stakes.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Square baskets begin with an interlaced grid of flat reed stakes clamped securely during bottom layout. Scoring the stakes allows clean 90-degree bends before side weavers build straight vertical walls.

sub_requirements.fact: An odd spoke count is required so each row alternates over and under successive stakes.
sub_requirements.misconception: Even spoke counts work properly for continuous single-weaver over-and-under round basket weaving.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Round baskets feature spokes radiating from a slotted wooden base or woven center button. Flexible round reed weavers build walls through continuous spiral randing or two-strand pairing.

sub_requirements.fact: Loose initial splint wrapping causes sagging and permanent seat failure under occupant weight.
sub_requirements.misconception: Splints can be wrapped loose because natural fiber shrinkage tightens the seat later.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Campstool seating uses wide flat ash or cane splints wrapped continuously around folding wooden rungs. Weaving the cross splints in a herringbone or twill pattern creates a durable, supportive seat.
